 'Bill has already been drafted': Legislators moving to quickly eliminate remaining 2% of grocery tax next session
 Austen Shipley 
 |
 10.16.26
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Tweet 
 Truth 
 Email 
 Print 
 (Photo via Austen Shipley/1819 News)
 HUNTSVILLE — A group of North Alabama Republican legislators pledged to eliminate the remaining 2% state sales tax on groceries during a Friday press conference at Star Super Market in Huntsville. 
 Officials in attendance included House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter (R-Rainsville), Senate President Pro Tem Garlan Gudger (R-Cullman), State Rep. Rex Reynolds (R-Hazel Green), State Sen. Sam Givhan (R-Huntsville), State Rep. James Lomax (R-Huntsville) and State Rep. Phillip Rigsby (R-Huntsville).
 Ledbetter told media members that a bill removing the final 2% of the tax has been drafted and will be introduced immediately, next session. 
 “It’s good to be in Huntsville today and to bring forth the fact that we're going to reduce the other 2% of grocery tax,” stated Ledbetter. “This past quadrennium , the gentlemen sitting behind us, the House and Senate members of Madison County, has reduced the taxes burden on Alabamians to the tune of over $1.5 billion dollars. The grocery tax is just part of that.”
 “Continuing to reduce and do away with the grocery tax is a huge savings to the people of Alabama, and we're happy to stand here today as a pledge to be able to do that. The bill has already been drafted, and we will be dropping it as soon as session begins to eliminate grocery tax on the people of this state.”

 Gudger echoed Ledbetter’s urgency on eliminating the remaining portion of the tax.
 “All of us here today, every Republican in Alabama running on office up and down the ticket, are committed to completely abolishing the grocery tax as quickly as possible,” said Gudger. “Cutting the grocery tax in half represents the largest tax cut in the history of Alabama, and removing the other half will set a new record that puts the unprecedented amounts of money back into the bank accounts of working families in every city, town, and crossroads across the state of Alabama.”
 He continued, “When the leadership of the House and Senate join together for an announcement, it is important and it demonstrates that we mean business. Alabamians will soon find their wallets a little bit fatter, their bank accounts a little bit more fuller as the savings that they keep, and as we send Republican team of lawmakers back to the state of Alabama for the legislature for this next session.”
 Reynolds, chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund Committee, referenced multiple residents in his district who have expressed unease about everyday expenses, including the cost of food. Reynolds believes that ending the last 2% of the grocery tax will ease some of those concerns. 
 “There's a lot going on in the district, and I tell you, it's so important and so timely for this leadership to stand behind us here today. Because I've been knocking on these doors and I've been talking to our neighbors, and they're concerned about this,” Reynolds said.
 “We talk about separating what's going on at the national level that's impacting our pricing and what we can control here in the state of Alabama," he added. "And this right here, we're doing it on top of the $1.5 billion dollars that we've already saved taxpayers.”
 Reynolds continued, “I tell people, people are making decisions between food and fuel, so this would be a great help for them.”
 Givhan called eliminating the final 2% significant for “kitchen table economics.”
 “It’s a tough time economically with the fuel prices that we have,” Givhan said. “What I paid just to fill up my truck the other day-that that stuff is real, and so the fact that we can get some relief here. Kitchen table economics is important, and I just appreciate that.”
 Rigsby also touted the expected outcome of removing the tax. 
 “We are proud to cut that extra 2% so that families in Alabama feel the impact, feel the difference, can take care of their families, can serve their families, can serve their communities by whatever we can do here locally to help those people,” stated Rigsby. 
 Lomax, who introduced a grocery tax holiday last session, explained how the state can afford to end the remaining tax.

 “We're going to make that holiday a permanent vacation,” Lomax said. “I know that it absolutely makes a difference fort Alabama families and people that I talk to each and every day.”
 He continued, “We've been able to grow our tax base in the state of Alabama by organically growing our business and industries, and recruiting industries from all across really the world to come here and help grow our tax base, so that we're able to grow the pie, and instead of taking pieces out of the pie and taking away those essential services.”
 “This is just one of those things that is built on the backs of smart people looking generations ahead and taking care of a better tomorrow today," Lomax outlined.
 According to Ledbetter, for a family spending $1,000 per month on qualifying groceries, eliminating the remaining 2% state tax would mean an additional $240 in annual savings. Combined with the reductions already enacted, that family would save approximately $480 annually compared with the original 4% state grocery tax.
 The Petroleum and Convenience Marketers of Alabama, a nonprofit trade association, issued its full support for ending the state grocery tax shortly after the legislators’ announcement.
 “In many rural areas of the state, convenience stores are the closest retailer of grocery items,” said Neal Morrison, director of governmental affairs for P&CMA. “We applaud the legislative leadership for continuing to push this plan, which will bring measurable and much-needed relief to families all across Alabama. We look forward to working with all members of the Alabama House and Senate to get this bill across the finish line in 2027.”
